API Security

Core controls for protecting public and internal APIs, with examples and a conceptual rate-limiter lab.

In this lesson

Why APIs are attacked, how to use keys and tokens, validation, and an architecture pattern to centralize controls.

A single leaked key or missing validation can expose user data or enable denial-of-service. Defensive design reduces blast radius.

Layered controls reduce attack surface and let services remain stateless when appropriate.

Handles TLS, authentication, rate limiting, and routing to services.
Tokens & Claims
Signed claims let services trust identity without constant lookups.
Validation & Encoding
Server-side checks and escaping protect data in transit and at render time.

screens.title: APIs as an Attack Surface
screens.narratorSegment: APIs are the programmable surface of your system. That makes them the natural place attackers look for sensitive data, ways to abuse resources, or entry points for injection attacks. Defending APIs means treating every public or internal endpoint as untrusted input. Start by defining what is being exposed: a product catalog, user profiles, order endpoints. Each endpoint has different sensitivity and therefore different controls. For example, a public catalog might only need an A P I key and generous rate limits, while an order placement endpoint needs strict authentication, lower rate limits, and careful validation. A common misconception is that 'internal' APIs are safe; in microservices, internal traffic can still be intercepted or misconfigured. So, assume any endpoint could be probed and apply least privilege, transport encryption, and per-endpoint controls. Test your A P I surface by listing endpoints, expected clients, and what data each should and should not return. That list drives decisions about keys, tokens, and gateway policies. Ask yourself: if this endpoint were called by a malicious client, what would be the worst outcome, and what control stops it?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › APIs as an Attack Surface
Definition

API attack surface

Any exposed endpoint, parameter, or data field that an external or internal client can reach.

Quick checklist
  • Catalog endpoints: public reads, low sensitivity.
  • Order endpoints: write actions, high sensitivity.
  • Admin endpoints: require strict auth and audit logging.
Common misconception

Internal endpoints are not automatically safe. Treat inter-service calls as needing authentication and encryption.

Endpoint catalog example
GET /products
Public catalog reads: API key identification, higher rate limits acceptable.
POST /orders
Creates purchases: requires authenticated user token, strict validation, low rate limit.
GET /user/profile
Private user data: strict auth, do not leak extra fields in responses.
PUT /admin/settings
Admin API: very restrictive access, audit and multi-factor checks recommended.
Key Takeaway

Classify endpoints and apply controls that match each endpoint's sensitivity and expected client set.

screens.title: API Keys: Uses and Limits
screens.narratorSegment: A P I keys are simple tokens that identify a client or application. They are useful for tracking usage and enabling rate limiting tied to a known client. For example, an e-commerce product lookup A P I might allow 100 requests per minute per A P I key for catalog reads while order placement is limited to five requests per minute. However, A P I keys are often transmitted in plain text and can be discovered in client-side code or logs. They are not designed to prove user identity because keys represent a client application, not a specific person. A common error is relying on A P I keys to authorize user-level actions. For user-specific access, use user-scoped tokens such as JWTs issued after authentication. When designing with A P I keys, plan for rotation, avoid embedding keys in public clients, and combine them with rate limiting and monitoring. Ask: if a key is leaked, what operations should be blocked and how quickly can you revoke it? API Keys: Uses and Limits means use keys for identification, billing, and throttling; do not treat them as user authentication.. In practical terms, client identification, analytics, and when a key is not enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › API Keys: Uses and Limits
When to use

Client identification and throttling

Issue API keys to third-party apps or server clients to attribute requests for analytics, billing, or rate limiting. Keys are simple and lightweight.

Benefits
  • Easy to issue and check.
  • Useful for per-client rate limits and billing.
  • Minimal server-side state required.
Limitations
  • Often static and can be leaked.
  • Do not prove a specific user's identity.
  • Insufficient alone for sensitive operations.
Example
Throttle policy example
Catalog reads: 100 requests per minute per API key. Place order: 5 requests per minute per API key. Monitor spikes and allow emergency revocation.
Misuse to avoid

Do not use API keys as the sole protection for user-specific data. If a key is compromised, attackers can act as the client application.

Pro Tip

Combine API keys with stricter auth for sensitive endpoints; require user tokens for user-scoped actions.

screens.title: Rate Limiting Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Rate limiting enforces a maximum number of requests a client may make in a time window. It protects resources from abuse and prevents brute-force and denial-of-service patterns. A simple flow is: assign a client identifier (A P I key or IP), track recent request timestamps, remove timestamps older than the window, and allow or block the request based on the remaining count. For instance, allow five login attempts per IP per 60 seconds to prevent credential-stuffing. Many implementations differ in how they count and expire entries, but the conceptual steps remain the same. When designing limits, choose different thresholds per endpoint according to sensitivity and expected usage patterns. Monitor blocked requests and tune thresholds to reduce false positives. A common mistake is setting a global low limit that breaks legitimate high-throughput clients; instead, apply per-endpoint, per-client, or per-key limits and provide separate higher-rate allowances for trusted partners. Rate Limiting Basics means throttle by client and endpoint, prune old data, and tune thresholds based on usage patterns.. In practical terms, how to throttle requests to protect resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Throttle by client and endpoint, prune old data, and tune thresholds based on usage patterns.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Rate Limiting Basics
Step-by-step
  1. Identify client key: API key, user id, or IP address.
  2. Record request timestamp for that client.
  3. Prune timestamps older than the time window.
  4. If remaining count >= limit, block; otherwise allow and record.
Configuration
Choose per-endpoint limits. Example: GET /products = 100/min per key. POST /orders = 5/min per key. Log blocked events for investigation.
Concrete example
A login endpoint allows 5 attempts per IP per 60 seconds. If a client sends a sixth attempt within the window, the API returns a rate-limited response and logs the event for monitoring.
Common mistake

Applying identical limits to all endpoints can block legitimate traffic; tune limits by endpoint and client trust.

screens.title: Conceptual Rate Limiter — Python Example
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a simple conceptual Python rate limiter. This in-memory example stores request timestamps per IP and prunes timestamps older than the time window. It then checks the remaining count and either allows or blocks the request. This is not a production-ready Redis-backed design, but it makes the logic explicit so you can reason about correctness and edge cases. For example, using a list of timestamps means pruning cost grows with rate; in production you might use a deque or a fixed-size counter with sliding-window approximations. A common misconception is that in-memory approaches are sufficient for distributed services; they do not share state across instances, which can let attackers bypass limits by distributing requests across machines. After reading the code, consider how you would make this resilient: central state, eviction, and consistent hashing are starting points. Try the conceptual test loop: make several requests and observe when the limiter blocks additional attempts. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Conceptual Rate Limiter
Concept

Timestamps per client

Store recent request times, prune old entries, then allow or block based on count.

Notes
  • Simple and explicit for single-process servers.
  • Production requires shared counters, sliding-window algorithms, or token buckets.
  • Log blocked events for incident response and tuning.
Conceptual Python
import time
from collections import defaultdict

request_timestamps = defaultdict(list)
RATE_LIMIT = 5  # Max requests
TIME_WINDOW = 60  # Seconds

def check_rate_limit(ip_address: str) -> bool:
    current_time = time.time()

    # 1. Keep only recent timestamps
    request_timestamps[ip_address] = [
        ts for ts in request_timestamps[ip_address]
        if ts > current_time - TIME_WINDOW
    ]

    # 2. Block if at or above the limit
    if len(request_timestamps[ip_address]) >= RATE_LIMIT:
        print(f"IP {ip_address} rate limited. Too many requests.")
        return False
    else:
        # 3. Record current timestamp and allow
        request_timestamps[ip_address].append(current_time)
        print(f"IP {ip_address} request allowed. Count: {len(request_timestamps[ip_address])}")
        return True
This example is the chapter's conceptual lab. Replace the in-memory store when you need cross-instance correctness.

screens.title: JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)
screens.narratorSegment: A JSON Web Token, or JWT, is a compact, URL-safe representation of claims that can be transferred between parties. It has three parts separated by dots: header, payload, and signature. The header says the token type and the signing algorithm as metadata. The payload contains claims such as user id, roles, issued-at time, and expiration. The signature proves the token was issued by a trusted party and that the content has not been changed. Because the server can validate the signature and read claims without a database lookup, JWTs are useful for stateless authentication and microservice authorization. A concrete example is issuing a token after login, then including it as a bearer token in the Authorization header of subsequent requests. A common misconception is that a JWT is encrypted by default; it is not. If you include sensitive data in the payload, you must encrypt it separately or avoid putting secrets there. Always verify signatures and check expiration before trusting claims. JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) means jwts carry claims and a signature so services can validate identity without per-request database lookups.. In practical terms, structure, claims, and why they enable stateless auth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)
Structure
Header · Payload · Signature. Header declares algorithm, payload has claims, signature verifies integrity.
Example payload
{ "sub": "1234567890", "name": "John Doe", "admin": true, "iat": 1516239022, "exp": 1516242622 }
Sign the token with a secret or private key; verify signature before trusting any claim. Always check expiration.
Usage
After authentication, issue a JWT and send it in the Authorization header as a bearer token. Services validate signature and extract claims for authorization decisions.
Misconception

A JWT is not encrypted by default; do not store secrets in the payload unless you encrypt the token payload.

Key Takeaway

JWTs are ideal for stateless auth when you can validate signatures and enforce short expirations and revocation strategies.

screens.title: Bearer Tokens and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: A typical server-side verification process takes the token from the Authorization header, validates the signature using the agreed algorithm, checks claims such as expiration and audience, and then extracts the user id and roles for authorization. The server must reject tokens with invalid signatures or expired timestamps. A danger is trusting expired tokens or tokens from a different issuer; always validate the issuer, audience, and the expiration claim. In the live coding demo you will see how a server receives a bearer token and validates it before allowing access. Pay attention to the verification step: signature check confirms integrity, and claim checks ensure the token was intended for this service. A common pitfall is to skip expiration checks or to accept tokens without verifying signatures, which defeats the purpose of using JWTs for secure stateless authentication. Bearer Tokens and Verification means always verify signature and check standard claims like exp and aud before using token claims for authorization.. In practical terms, how an api verifies and extracts claims from a jwt. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Bearer Tokens and Verification
Flow
  1. Client sends Authorization: Bearer <token> header.
  2. Server parses token and validates signature with secret or public key.
  3. Server checks expiration, issuer, and audience claims.
  4. If valid, extract subject and roles to authorize the request.
Make sure revocation and short expirations are part of your strategy so compromised tokens have limited lifespan.
Verification example
// Pseudocode
// 1. Extract token from header
// 2. Verify signature using server key
// 3. Check exp and aud claims
// 4. Use claims to authorize
Pitfall

Do not treat JWTs as proof of freshness without checking the expiration and optionally keeping a short TTL or revocation list.

screens.title: Input Validation and Output Encoding
screens.narratorSegment: Input validation and output encoding are foundational for A P I security. Input validation means checking every incoming value against expected formats, types, and constraints. That prevents malformed or malicious payloads from reaching downstream systems and reduces the risk of S Q L injection or command injection. Output encoding means escaping or encoding data before it is rendered or sent to other systems so that data cannot be interpreted as executable code in a browser or another context. A concrete example from the chapter is a comment submission containing a script tag. Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Input Validation & Output Encoding
Input Validation

Check types, ranges, and acceptable characters on the server. Reject or sanitize anything unexpected.

Example
Reject raw HTML in comments, or sanitize by removing script tags and disallowed attributes.
Output Encoding

Encode special characters before sending to browsers or other interpreters so the content renders as text, not executable code.

Attack example and prevention
If a comment contains <script>...</script> and you save and render it verbatim, browsers will execute it. Validate to remove scripts and encode before rendering to prevent execution.
Key Takeaway

Never trust client input. Validate on the server and encode outputs for the target rendering context.

screens.title: API Gateway and Microservice Security
screens.narratorSegment: An A P I Gateway acts as the single entry point for client requests, centralizing authentication, authorization, rate limiting, SSL termination, and input validation. By placing these controls at the gateway, individual microservices can remain simpler and less error-prone, because many checks happen before the request reaches them. For example, the gateway can verify JWT signatures, apply per-key rate limits, and reject malformed payloads. This reduces the likelihood that a service will accidentally expose sensitive data or miss critical checks. For inter-service communication, ensure encryption and strong service identity; the chapter suggests patterns like mutual TLS for secure channels. A common mistake is relying on gateways alone and not implementing defense in depth. While the gateway does much, critical authorization checks that depend on business logic should still be enforced by the service that owns the data. Use the gateway to stop most bad traffic and services to enforce fine-grained data authorization. Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › API Gateway and Microservice Security
Role of an API Gateway
Authentication
Validate credentials, verify JWTs and issue short-lived tokens if needed.
Rate Limiting
Apply per-client and per-endpoint throttles to protect downstream services.
Input Validation
Reject malformed payloads and enforce schemas before forwarding requests.
Gateway example
Clients call the gateway, which enforces TLS, validates tokens, applies rate limits, and routes to microservices. Services then trust the gateway for transport-level checks but still enforce business-level authorization.
Pitfall

Do not delegate every authorization check to the gateway. Services must still validate critical, data-level permissions.

screens.title: Common API Security Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Designers and engineers frequently make similar mistakes that increase risk. First, exposing sensitive data in A P I responses happens when endpoints return too much context; ensure you only return what the client needs. Second, weak or missing authentication allows unauthorized access; enforce strong authentication for every endpoint that handles sensitive actions. Third, insufficient rate limiting leaves doors open for brute-force and DoS attacks; apply per-client and per-endpoint limits. Fourth, failing to validate input leads to injection and XSS vulnerabilities; validate inputs server-side and encode outputs. Fifth, hardcoding A P I keys in client-side code makes them trivially discoverable; always keep keys secret and provide short-lived credentials to clients when needed. Finally, forgetting authorization checks on every call can let authenticated clients access others' data; validate claims and scopes per request. The antidote is layered defenses, centralized policies at the gateway, and careful code reviews focused on these risky areas. Over-sharing data
Return minimal fields required by the client.
Weak authentication
Enforce strong user or client authentication on all sensitive endpoints.

Demo steps
  1. Start with Flask endpoint checking a hardcoded API key and returning JSON.

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

API_KEY = 'hardcoded-key'

@app.route('/products')
def products():
    key = request.headers.get('X-Api-Key')
    if key != API_KEY:
        return jsonify({'error':'unauthorized'}), 401
    return jsonify({'products': [...]})
This snippet is starter code for the demo. Never hardcode keys in production; use secrets management and rotation.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts. A P I keys provide client identification and support rate limiting but are not a substitute for user authentication. fullNarratorScript:
APIs connect users, services, and partners, which makes them both powerful and vulnerable. In this lesson you will learn core controls that reduce risk: simple client identification with A P I keys and traffic shaping with rate limiting; stateless authentication and claims with JSON Web Tokens; defensive input validation and output encoding to avoid injection and cross-site scripting; and a centralized A P I gateway pattern to enforce consistent security across microservices. You will see concrete examples, a conceptual rate-limiter implementation in Python, and practical assessment scenarios to test your understanding. A common misconception is that a single control fixes everything — in reality these techniques work together. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose when to issue an A P I key, when to issue a user-specific token, how to validate external input, and how an A P I gateway reduces duplicated security code across services. Think about a public product catalog and a protected order endpoint: they need different controls, and that contrast will guide many design decisions you make as a system designer.

These objectives frame practical skills you should leave with. First, you will recognize common security challenges and vulnerabilities in A P I design, so you can spot where protections are missing. Second, you will implement basic protections: issuing A P I keys for client identification and applying rate limiting to prevent abuse. Third, you will understand JSON Web Tokens — how a header, payload, and signature form a compact bearer token — and when JWTs are appropriate for stateless authentication and authorization. Fourth, you will apply input validation and output encoding practices to prevent injection and cross-site scripting. Each objective pairs a concept with a why: for example, using rate limiting prevents brute-force attacks, while validation stops malicious payloads before they reach your datastore. Keep these aims in mind as you follow the hands-on rate-limiter example and the JWT discussion; they tie the theory to real server-side checks you'll design for production APIs.

In this second objectives screen we translate aims into demonstrations. To show you can identify vulnerabilities, we will examine common mistakes such as exposing sensitive fields in responses. For A P I keys and rate limiting, you will design a throttle policy for two endpoints: a high-throughput catalog lookup and a low-throughput order placement endpoint. For JWTs, you will validate signatures and read claims to perform authorization without a database lookup on every request. For validation and encoding, you will sanitize a comment submission and then encode it before rendering to stop stored cross-site scripting. Each objective will be measured by a small task or check: a review of responses, a conceptual rate-limiter test, a token verification step, and a pair of validation/encoding checks. These applied targets help you move from understanding to practical skill quickly, and they mirror real engineering tasks you will perform during system design and code reviews.

APIs are the programmable surface of your system. That makes them the natural place attackers look for sensitive data, ways to abuse resources, or entry points for injection attacks. Defending APIs means treating every public or internal endpoint as untrusted input. Start by defining what is being exposed: a product catalog, user profiles, order endpoints. Each endpoint has different sensitivity and therefore different controls. For example, a public catalog might only need an A P I key and generous rate limits, while an order placement endpoint needs strict authentication, lower rate limits, and careful validation. A common misconception is that 'internal' APIs are safe; in microservices, internal traffic can still be intercepted or misconfigured. So, assume any endpoint could be probed and apply least privilege, transport encryption, and per-endpoint controls. Test your A P I surface by listing endpoints, expected clients, and what data each should and should not return. That list drives decisions about keys, tokens, and gateway policies. Ask yourself: if this endpoint were called by a malicious client, what would be the worst outcome, and what control stops it?

A P I keys are simple tokens that identify a client or application. They are useful for tracking usage and enabling rate limiting tied to a known client. For example, an e-commerce product lookup A P I might allow 100 requests per minute per A P I key for catalog reads while order placement is limited to five requests per minute. However, A P I keys are often transmitted in plain text and can be discovered in client-side code or logs. They are not designed to prove user identity because keys represent a client application, not a specific person. A common error is relying on A P I keys to authorize user-level actions. For user-specific access, use user-scoped tokens such as JWTs issued after authentication. When designing with A P I keys, plan for rotation, avoid embedding keys in public clients, and combine them with rate limiting and monitoring. Ask: if a key is leaked, what operations should be blocked and how quickly can you revoke it? API Keys: Uses and Limits means use keys for identification, billing, and throttling; do not treat them as user authentication.. In practical terms, client identification, analytics, and when a key is not enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Rate limiting enforces a maximum number of requests a client may make in a time window. It protects resources from abuse and prevents brute-force and denial-of-service patterns. A simple flow is: assign a client identifier (A P I key or IP), track recent request timestamps, remove timestamps older than the window, and allow or block the request based on the remaining count. For instance, allow five login attempts per IP per 60 seconds to prevent credential-stuffing. Many implementations differ in how they count and expire entries, but the conceptual steps remain the same. When designing limits, choose different thresholds per endpoint according to sensitivity and expected usage patterns. Monitor blocked requests and tune thresholds to reduce false positives. A common mistake is setting a global low limit that breaks legitimate high-throughput clients; instead, apply per-endpoint, per-client, or per-key limits and provide separate higher-rate allowances for trusted partners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we'll walk through a simple conceptual Python rate limiter. This in-memory example stores request timestamps per IP and prunes timestamps older than the time window. It then checks the remaining count and either allows or blocks the request. This is not a production-ready Redis-backed design, but it makes the logic explicit so you can reason about correctness and edge cases. For example, using a list of timestamps means pruning cost grows with rate; in production you might use a deque or a fixed-size counter with sliding-window approximations. A common misconception is that in-memory approaches are sufficient for distributed services; they do not share state across instances, which can let attackers bypass limits by distributing requests across machines. After reading the code, consider how you would make this resilient: central state, eviction, and consistent hashing are starting points. A JSON Web Token, or JWT, is a compact, URL-safe representation of claims that can be transferred between parties. It has three parts separated by dots: header, payload, and signature. The header says the token type and the signing algorithm as metadata. The payload contains claims such as user id, roles, issued-at time, and expiration. The signature proves the token was issued by a trusted party and that the content has not been changed. Because the server can validate the signature and read claims without a database lookup, JWTs are useful for stateless authentication and microservice authorization. A concrete example is issuing a token after login, then including it as a bearer token in the Authorization header of subsequent requests. A common misconception is that a JWT is encrypted by default; it is not. If you include sensitive data in the payload, you must encrypt it separately or avoid putting secrets there. Always verify signatures and check expiration before trusting claims. Let's summarize the essential concepts. A P I keys provide client identification and support rate limiting but are not a substitute for user authentication. Rate limiting protects endpoints from abuse and must be tuned per endpoint and client. JSON Web Tokens carry claims in a header, payload, and signature; validate signatures and expiration before using claims for authorization.
